who: the English botanist on Cook's first voyage (1743-1820)
why: He collected the Australian shrub on the Endeavour voyage.
mean: An Australian shrub with dense brush-like flower spikes
story: A wealthy young botanist paid his own way onto Cook's Endeavour and came home with fourteen hundred plants nobody in Europe had seen. He later ran Kew Gardens for four decades, and the bottlebrush-flowered shrub carries his name.

why: A botanist named the butterfly bush in his memory.
mean: A shrub with long spikes of flowers that attract butterflies
story: An English country rector spent his spare hours cataloguing mosses and grasses so carefully that Linnaeus later used his work. He never saw the shrub named for him: it came from China decades after his death, and now colonises railway sidings everywhere.

who: a Spanish vicereine of Peru said to have been cured by the bark
why: The malaria-treating bark took her title, though the story may be legend.
mean: A South American tree whose bark yields quinine
story: The bark of a Peruvian tree was the only cure for malaria for three centuries. Linnaeus named the genus after a vicereine said to have been saved by it, then misspelled her title. The story is probably invented; the spelling error certainly was not.

why: A botanist friend named the scented bulb after him.
mean: A scented South African flower grown from a corm
story: A German botanist collecting in South Africa found a small scented flower on a one-sided spike and named it after a doctor friend back home. It became one of the most popular cut flowers in the world on the strength of its smell alone.

why: A botanist named the daisy in his honour after his early death.
mean: A large brightly coloured daisy from South Africa
story: A German doctor ran a botanical garden in Moscow and explored the Volga collecting plants before dying at thirty-three. A colleague named a South African daisy after him, and it is now the fifth most sold cut flower on earth.

why: The bell-flowered houseplant was named for him.
mean: A houseplant with large velvety bell-shaped flowers
story: A German botanist writing in the 1780s had a genus of velvet-flowered tropical plants named after him. Confusingly, the plant sold in shops under his name today belongs to a different genus entirely, which botanists have given up trying to correct.

who: a British collector and founder of the Royal Horticultural Society (1749-1809)
why: A botanist named the Australian genus after him.
mean: An Australian shrub with brush-like or spider-like flowers
story: A British collector who helped found the Royal Horticultural Society had a large Australian genus named after him. There are over three hundred and fifty species, from ground creepers to trees, and almost all of them are pollinated by birds rather than insects.

who: the British colonial official who founded Singapore (1781-1826)
why: The giant parasitic flower was named after him by its describer.
mean: A parasitic plant bearing the largest single flower on earth
story: The plant has no leaves, no stem and no roots. It lives inside a vine and erupts as a metre-wide reddish flower that smells of rotting meat to draw flies. It was named for the colonial official who founded Singapore.

who: a Russian grand duchess who became Queen of the Netherlands (1795-1865)
why: A Dutch-funded expedition named the tree after their queen.
mean: A fast-growing tree with large leaves and purple bell flowers
story: A German botanist working for the Dutch named a Japanese tree after the Russian grand duchess who had become Queen of the Netherlands. It grows faster than almost any hardwood, up to five metres in a single season.

who: the American explorer of the Lewis and Clark expedition (1774-1809)
why: A botanist named the alpine flower from specimens he collected.
mean: A low alpine plant with fleshy leaves and bright flowers
story: An American explorer crossing the Rockies collected a low plant with fleshy leaves whose root the local tribes ate. It survived being pressed, dried and carried across a continent, and then sprouted in a Philadelphia garden.

who: the American explorer of the Lewis and Clark expedition (1770-1838)
why: The wildflower was named for the second leader of the expedition.
mean: A North American wildflower with fringed pink or purple petals
story: The other leader of the great American overland expedition got his name on a genus of showy pink wildflowers found along the route. His companion got a different plant, so the two men who crossed the continent together are commemorated in separate genera.

who: the Swedish botanist who invented modern biological naming (1707-1778)
why: He chose a small modest twinflower to carry his own name.
mean: A small creeping woodland plant with paired pink bell flowers
story: The man who named tens of thousands of species reserved one for himself, and pointedly chose a tiny creeping woodland plant with two nodding pink bells. A colleague wrote that it was lowly, insignificant and flowered only briefly, like its namesake.

why: The flowering shrub was named in his honour.
mean: A garden shrub with trumpet-shaped pink or red flowers
story: A German chemistry professor who also taught botany had an East Asian flowering shrub named after him. Robert Fortune brought it out of China in the 1840s on the same journeys that smuggled tea plants to India.

who: an English horticulturist and orchid collector (1788-1835)
why: He coaxed a discarded orchid into flower and it was named for him.
mean: A showy tropical orchid with large frilled flowers
story: An English collector was sent a crate of Brazilian mosses packed in what looked like dead stems. He planted the packing material anyway. It flowered into an orchid nobody had seen, and the genus took his name.

who: a Finnish-Swedish botanist and student of Linnaeus (1716-1779)
why: Linnaeus named the North American shrub after his travelling student.
mean: An evergreen shrub with clusters of cup-shaped flowers
story: Linnaeus sent a student to North America to find plants that might survive Swedish winters. He came back with an evergreen shrub whose stamens are spring-loaded and fling pollen at visiting bees. Linnaeus named it after him.

who: a Scottish physician and patron of Linnaeus (died 1747)
why: Linnaeus named the henna plant after the man who funded his great work.
mean: The shrub whose leaves yield the reddish dye henna
story: A Scottish army physician paid the printing costs of the book in which Linnaeus first laid out his system of classification. In return Linnaeus named the henna shrub after him, so the dye on a thousand years of hands carries a Scot's surname.

why: The pitcher plant genus was named after him.
mean: A carnivorous plant with tube-shaped leaves that trap insects
story: A French surgeon in Quebec sent European botanists a plant whose leaves form tall tubes half full of liquid. Insects walk in on downward-pointing hairs and cannot climb out. The genus was named after him.

why: The false acacia was named after the gardener who first grew it in Europe.
mean: A thorny North American tree with hanging white flower clusters
story: A gardener to three French kings planted a North American tree in Paris around 1601. One of the specimens he or his son planted is still alive, propped on crutches, making it the oldest tree in the city.

why: Linnaeus named the air plants after him as a joke about water.
mean: An air plant that takes moisture from the air rather than soil
story: A Finnish botanist was so violently seasick on one voyage that he walked home round the Gulf of Bothnia instead. Linnaeus, who found this funny, gave his name to a genus of plants that seem to repel water and live on air.

who: a Baltic German naturalist and ship's surgeon (1793-1831)
why: A shipmate named the California poppy after him.
mean: The California poppy, with silky orange cup-shaped flowers
story: A Baltic German ship's surgeon sailed round the world twice on Russian expeditions. His friend and shipmate named the golden poppy of the Californian hills after him, saddling the state flower with one of the hardest genus names in botany.

why: The trailing rock plant was named after the artist.
mean: A low trailing rock plant with dense purple flowers
story: A French botanical artist who drew plants on expeditions to the Levant had a low cushion-forming rock plant named after him. It is the sheet of purple that spills over garden walls in April.

why: The giant-leaved genus was named after him.
mean: A plant with enormous rhubarb-like leaves
story: A Norwegian bishop who catalogued his country's flora between sermons had a genus named after him whose largest species carries leaves three metres across, big enough to shelter under. Nothing in Norway grows remotely like it.

why: The red hot poker plant was named after him.
mean: A tall African plant with a spike of red and yellow tubular flowers
story: A German physician published books illustrated by pressing inked plants straight onto the page. A South African plant whose flower spike burns from red at the top to yellow at the bottom was later named after him.

why: Linnaeus named the aromatic herb after him.
mean: An aromatic North American herb, also called bergamot
story: A Spanish physician in Seville wrote the first European account of the plants coming back from the Americas, including tobacco and sunflowers, without ever crossing the Atlantic himself. Linnaeus named a fragrant mint-family herb after him.

why: He sent the African violet's seed to his botanist father.
mean: The African violet, a small houseplant with velvety leaves
story: A German administrator in East Africa found a small purple flower growing in the shade of a rock and posted seed home to his father. It became one of the most popular houseplants in the world, and the genus took the family name.

who: a British sealing captain and navigator (1787-1834)
why: He sailed further south than anyone had and both a sea and a seal took his name.
mean: An Antarctic seal that dives deeper and longer than any other
story: A British sealing captain pushed his ship further south than anyone before him through an unusually ice-free summer. The sea he found and the seal that lives in it both took his name; the seal can hold its breath for eighty minutes.

who: a Russian explorer of Central Asia (1839-1888)
why: He described the last truly wild horse.
mean: The last surviving species of wild horse, native to the Mongolian steppe
story: A Russian explorer brought back a skull and hide from the Mongolian steppe that proved a genuinely wild horse still existed, never domesticated. It went extinct in the wild in the 1960s and was brought back from twelve captive animals.

who: a German naturalist on the Russian Bering expedition (1709-1746)
why: He described a sea cow, a jay, a sea eagle and a sea lion in a few weeks.
mean: Describing several North Pacific animals recorded by one naturalist
story: A German naturalist got ten hours ashore in Alaska and used them so well that six species now carry his name. He described a nine-metre sea cow that was hunted to extinction within twenty-seven years of his sighting it.

who: the wife of a French Antarctic explorer
why: Her husband named a stretch of Antarctic coast, and its penguin, after her.
mean: A small black-and-white Antarctic penguin
story: A French explorer charting the Antarctic coast named the land he found after his wife, waiting at home in France. The small penguins nesting on it took the same name, so the commonest penguin in Antarctica is called after a Frenchwoman who never went there.

who: a German city and grand duchy
why: The grand duke's court bred the grey hunting dog.
mean: A large sleek grey hunting dog with pale eyes
story: The court of a German grand duchy bred a grey gundog for hunting big game, then kept the bloodline closed to outsiders for a century. When Americans finally got some in the 1920s, the breed carried the duchy's name.

who: a large island off eastern Canada
why: The heavy water-rescue dog was bred there by fishermen.
mean: A very large gentle dog bred for water rescue
story: Fishermen on a cold Canadian island bred an enormous dog with webbed feet and a waterproof coat to haul nets and pull drowning men out of the surf. One is recorded as having saved twenty people from a single wreck.

who: an ancient city in southern Arabia
why: The desert hunting hound is thought to take its name from the town.
mean: A slender long-haired hunting hound of the Middle East
story: A slender hound bred to run down gazelle across open desert appears in Egyptian tomb paintings four thousand years old. Bedouin tribes let them sleep in the tent, an honour no other dog received, and their name traces to an Arabian town.

why: Mill workers in the valley bred the large terrier.
mean: The largest of the terrier breeds, with a wiry tan and black coat
story: Mill workers in a Yorkshire river valley crossed terriers with otterhounds to get a dog that could hunt on land and in water. It grew into the largest terrier of all, and served as a messenger dog in the trenches of the First World War.

why: The first show cats of the breed were said to have come from there.
mean: A short-haired cat with a distinctive ticked coat
story: A cat shown in London in 1871 was billed as having been brought back from an Ethiopian campaign. The claim is doubtful and the breed's real origins are probably Indian Ocean coastal, but the country's old name stuck to it.

why: The genus of animal-borne bacteria was named in his honour.
mean: A genus of bacteria causing infections often caught from animal bites
story: The Frenchman who proved germs cause disease had a whole genus named after him: rod-shaped bacteria that live harmlessly in cats' and dogs' mouths and cause fast, angry infections in bitten humans.

who: a Belgian immunologist and Nobel laureate (1870-1961)
why: He isolated the whooping cough bacterium.
mean: A genus of bacteria including the cause of whooping cough
story: A Belgian immunologist grew the whooping cough organism from his own infant son's cough in 1906. He won a Nobel Prize for separate work on how blood destroys bacteria, and the genus carries his name.

why: He identified the bacterium causing gonorrhoea.
mean: A genus of paired bacteria including the causes of gonorrhoea and meningitis
story: A German bacteriologist aged twenty-four identified the coffee-bean-shaped paired bacteria behind one venereal disease, staining them from patients own samples. The same genus includes the organism that causes the most feared and fastest-moving form of bacterial meningitis.

why: The corkscrew-shaped bacteria were named in his honour.
mean: A genus of corkscrew-shaped bacteria including the cause of Lyme disease
story: A French bacteriologist gave his name to a genus of loosely coiled corkscrew bacteria. One species, carried by ticks that feed on deer and mice, causes Lyme disease and can hide in the body for years.

why: An outbreak at their 1976 convention revealed the organism.
mean: A genus of waterborne bacteria causing a severe pneumonia
story: In 1976 a hundred and eighty delegates at a veterans' convention in Philadelphia fell ill and thirty-four died. It took six months to trace it to bacteria breeding in the hotel's cooling tower, and the organism took the delegates' name.

why: The intestinal parasite was named in his honour.
mean: A pear-shaped intestinal parasite causing persistent diarrhoea
story: A French zoologist had a pear-shaped single-celled parasite named after him. It clamps onto the lining of the small intestine with a sucking disc, and hikers who drink from clear mountain streams have been discovering it ever since.

who: a Scottish pathologist and army officer (1865-1926)
why: He identified the parasite behind a fatal tropical fever.
mean: A genus of parasites spread by sandflies, causing skin and organ disease
story: A Scottish army pathologist found tiny bodies in the spleen of a soldier dead of a wasting Indian fever. The parasite is spread by sandflies, and in its worst form it destroys the liver and spleen and kills within two years.

why: The insect-infecting bacteria were named after him.
mean: A genus of bacteria that live inside insect cells and alter their reproduction
story: An American pathologist gave his name to bacteria living inside the cells of most insect species on earth. They manipulate their hosts' reproduction so thoroughly that scientists now use them deliberately to stop mosquitoes carrying dengue.

who: an Italian physicist and steamboat pioneer (18th century)
why: An Italian pharmacist named the red-pigmented bacteria after his countryman.
mean: A genus of bacteria, one species of which produces a red pigment
story: An Italian pharmacist investigating why polenta turned blood-red overnight found a bacterium making a scarlet pigment, and named it after a countryman he thought had been cheated of credit for the steamboat. It is now a serious hospital infection.

who: a German physician and Nobel laureate (1854-1915)
why: The tick-borne bacteria were named in his honour.
mean: A genus of tick-borne bacteria that infect white blood cells
story: The German who invented chemotherapy and the first cure for syphilis had a genus of tick-borne bacteria named after him. They hide inside the very white blood cells sent to destroy them, which is why the infection is so hard to spot.

why: He isolated the branching bacteria from cattle disease.
mean: A genus of branching soil bacteria causing lung and skin infection
story: A French veterinarian isolated a branching, thread-like bacterium from cattle on Guadeloupe. It lives in soil and dust and mostly troubles people whose immune systems are already failing, which is why it became far better known after 1980.

why: He identified the blood parasite in cattle.
mean: A genus of tick-borne parasites that destroy red blood cells
story: A Romanian bacteriologist found parasites inside the red blood cells of cattle with a wasting fever. It was the first proof that a tick could carry disease, and the discovery reshaped how doctors thought about insects entirely.

why: The cattle blood parasite was named after him.
mean: A genus of tick-borne parasites causing fatal cattle disease
story: A Swiss veterinarian who lost an arm in an accident became the founding figure of South African veterinary science. The tick-borne parasite named after him kills cattle across east and southern Africa, and shaped the whole continent's livestock trade.

why: He found the worm larvae behind elephantiasis.
mean: A genus of thread-like worms that block lymph vessels
story: A German physician working in Brazil found thread-like worm larvae in the urine of patients with grotesquely swollen limbs. The adult worms clog the lymph vessels, and the disease they cause still affects tens of millions of people.
